content.thinking:
I'm working out the precise geometry for the slab's tiered structure, setting dimensions and vertical positions for the lower and upper tiers before placing the overall model within its bounding box.

Now I'm laying out the pole's vertical structure: a gold collar at the socket, curved claws gripping the slab base, then spine-like vertebrae segments spaced along the shaft with increasing spike lengths as they rise toward the skull.

Each vertebra is a tapered cylinder with bone coloring, flanked by small transverse-process wings and a neural spine jutting outward at a slight downward angle, with the spike base sized to fit inside the cylinder radius.

Still writing geometry...

Still plotting ribbon sway points...

I need to shorten the ribbon so it doesn't collide with the vertebrae spikes, ending it around y=0.82 instead of lower. Then I'm positioning the soul spiral around the pole, spanning y=0.5 to 1.72, with three and a half turns clearing the spike radius.

Checking the spiral against the talon collar, I'm widening its radius to 0.17 to stay clear of claw and spike geometry, and adding a glowing tube with five orbs placed along the path. Now I'm defining the blade spine control points as an array of offset coordinates building the blade's curved outline.

Still writing blade geometry...

No smoothing, keeping facets polygonal for a low-poly look with one mirrored side. I'm adding a glowing edge strip swept along the tip curve, then setting up the plate's paint function using distance from the spine normalized by width to drive the banding pattern.

Writing banding color logic...

Now I'm shaping the spine as a tapering tube path with rounded caps using bone-colored paint, then adding small vertebra knobs spaced along it, and planning spur elements positioned at points along the spine.

Still writing spike and flame placement logic...

Working through this, the plane spanned by width and Z would make the card appear edge-on to a viewer looking along Z, which defeats the purpose of flame cards facing the camera. I need cards that face ±Z while leaning toward the flow direction, but that combination isn't achievable with this particular construction—facing Z and leaning along −T are mutually exclusive here.

Thinking about the cross-card option instead: with `cross: true`, a second card gets added at right angles through the spine axis, so if both cards lean the same way, the cross card's plane contains the leaned spine direction and a perpendicular width, which could give the front-facing view I actually want.

Writing SVG flame path...

Writing flame path coordinates...

Adding gold spine rings and placing rune glyphs along the plate, scaling glyph size relative to local plate width so they fit proportionally at each position.

Now I'm sketching a skull-building helper function that takes position, scale, yaw, and jaw angle parameters, with closures for rotating and placing points in local space to construct the geometry.

Still defining skull shapes...

Setting round caps where the snout meets the cranium and flat caps at the tip for a blunt box shape. I'm adding a nose pad sphere with dark nostril ellipses, then placing upper teeth as a series along the snout with decreasing width per tooth.

Working out the lower jaw edge and tooth geometry, giving the fang at index 2 extra length and radius, building each tooth as a spike primitive with pentagonal cross-section. Computing the snout's half-width taper from base to tip so tooth placement scales correctly along that curve.

Now I'm setting up the jaw pivot and rotation frame so mandible points can be defined locally then transformed into world space, then sweeping the mandible rami as tapered rods from the jaw joint to the chin, with a thicker rod joining the two sides at the chin.

Then I'm lofting the underjaw as a solid tapering shape from wide near the joint to narrow at the chin, replacing the separate rami approach, and adding lower teeth as small rotated spikes along the top edge using the same jaw-local coordinate helper for consistency.

Thinking about the mouth interior, I decide a dark roof plate underneath the snout would add contrast but mostly skip detailed interior geometry since it's only visible from certain angles. Moving to the eyes, I'm placing socket ellipsoids angled outward with a glowing sphere inset for the eye itself.

Adding brow ridges and spike horns, I'm sweeping a rod from the forehead back toward the rear with tapering radius, then adding a small spike horn jutting up and back. For the main horns, I'm sketching a curved sweep with multiple control points from base to tip, angling outward on both sides.

Shaping the horn tip with a point cap, and painting it with a gradient so the very tip gets a distinct color, then gold near the base, then bone color beneath. I'm considering adding ridge bands along the horn for texture but thinking it might be simpler to skip the extra cylinders and just paint color bands instead.

Now I'm sketching secondary smaller horns using a quadratic bezier curve with tapering radius, then laying out cheek spikes by positioning tip and base points for each spike per side, and starting on crest spikes running along the midline.

Still working out positions...

Still adding gem and trim details...

I'm scattering small decorative elements across the slab too -- pebbles, a few soul crystal shards near the skull and rune, all using the same chamfered rectangle path function for consistency, and setting up the stone material with mottled color variation for texture.

Now I'm defining the flagstone paving pattern using patches of varying blue-purple tones for a runic stone surface, then positioning bone-arc ribs behind the trophy skull, placing it at roughly x=0.55, z=0.12 with a yaw rotation for the facing angle.

I'm working out the skull's spatial geometry at scale 1.7 — calculating where the cranium origin, snout tip, and horn tips land after applying the yaw rotation, checking whether the horns' back position collides with a nearby pole.

Reducing trophy scale to 1.25 solves the collision — recalculating the horn tips and snout tip positions confirms they now fit cleanly within the slab's depth bounds and stay clear of the pole.

Checking the skull height and cranium placement, and then working out where to position the ribs — since they'd conflict with the horns if placed directly behind the skull, I'm shifting the plan to arrange three standing "tusk" ribs off to the right-back instead.

Actually, I'll place the ribcage arching from the slab at the right side, curving upward and back toward the left like a fan of half-buried bones, with three ribs of varying height and tapering radius. I'm also adding a scattering of vertebrae cylinders lying near the front-left for added detail.

Now I'm setting up the builder structure—defining the root joint position, attaching geometry parts like cylinders oriented along custom directions, and writing typed color helpers for the grip paint, making sure everything passes strict typechecking with no unused imports.

Defining the spine points...

I'm realizing the resulting blade length comes out to around 2 meters when summed across the segments, which feels oversized compared to a real scythe blade's typical 0.8-1m length -- but given the exaggerated style this might be intentional.

I'll scale down the spine points to get a more reasonable ~1.6m blade chord, then work out the pole offset PX needed so the overall silhouette stays centered given the horn positions and blade bounding box.

Total height checks out around 2.4 with pole top near 1.95, so that's fine. Now I'm computing a width profile function that tapers along the spine, finding its maximum around 0.19 to make sure the plate fits within the curvature, then setting up sampling points for the blade offset along the plate from t=0.04 to 1.

Checking whether the plate's start overlaps the skull's snout — it does, but since the plate sits inside the mouth near the jaw region, that overlap is acceptable as an embedded/held placement rather than a collision.

Now I'm writing the code for the chamfered rectangle outline that defines the slab's shape, then extruding that outline into a 3D slab with stone-colored side faces.

I'm working out the paint logic so the top face and side faces get different cel-shaded tones based on their surface normals relative to the light direction, giving lit versus shadowed edges a believable variation.

Now I'm adding decorative details: a gold rim border along the tier1 top edge, plus carved bone claw feet positioned at the chamfered corners of the slab's lower tier, computing their base and tip coordinates from the slab's half-width and half-depth dimensions.

For the orbs and wisps along the spiral path, I'm placing glowing spheres at sampled points, with trailing tail spikes pointing backward along the spiral direction and small dark eye spheres offset outward from each orb's center.

I'm defining the spiral geometry parameters—center, turns, radius, pitch—keeping the radius constant since start and end values match, and checking the glow intensity settings before moving to glyph decal textures rendered as SVG runes with glowing teal strokes.

Still writing SVG glyphs...

Now I'm working out the rune ring plane geometry placement, sizing it relative to the slab depth and orienting it to face upward correctly.

I'm also sizing the slab tiers and planning a teal inlay line inset from the perimeter at the proper height.

Now I'm checking the rune circle against the inlay chamfer to avoid overlap, settling on a smaller rune radius so it fits cleanly. Then I'm turning to the trophy skull's details—mouth flames, crystals, pebbles—and planning the TS part-building function signature to keep color typing consistent.

Writing skull builder code...

Checking the direction confirms it points downward as expected. Now I'm defining the mandible loft stations with progressively narrower width and height along the jaw, using hexagonal cross-sections with rounded start and flat end caps, then moving on to placing the lower teeth.

Working out positions for six lower teeth, each with a base and tip point scaled down in width going back along the jaw, skipping a cheek fill detail and considering whether to add a dark inner-mouth ellipse for depth (deciding to skip it for now). Then I start defining the bone color palette, including a mottled painted variant with hue-shifted shadow tones.

Still defining colors...

With palette settled, I'm tallying part counts—vertebrae segments with their spikes, claws, flame texture arrays—before writing the full file.
